We have carbon NMR peaks: 9 signals. Need number of methyl groups (CH3). Methyl carbon appears around 10-30 ppm typically. Here we have peaks at 43.30 and 26.29. 43 ppm could be a carbon attached to heteroatom (e.g., carbonyl adjacent). 26 ppm typical for methyl. Also maybe other methyls hidden if overlapping? Only two low-field peaks. Methyl groups give one carbon each. So likely 1 methyl (26.29). But could be two methyls: one at 26.29, another at 43.30 if it's a methyl attached to carbonyl (acetyl) ~30 ppm? Actually acetyl methyl (CH3CO) appears ~30 ppm. 43 ppm is more like a carbon attached to electronegative atom (e.g., O-CH3 ~55 ppm). So 43 could be OCH3. That's also methyl. So there may be two methyl carbons: 43.30 (OCH3) and 26.29 (alkyl methyl). So answer 2.

Check if any other data needed? Could also use proton NMR to confirm number of methyl protons. Let's get proton NMR.
